REFORMATION OF AN UNAMBIGUOUS WILL OR TRUST FOR MISTAKE (ESTATE OF DUKE; PROB. CODE §§ 631, 632, 825, 6111.5, 21102, 21120; ESTATE OF EIMERS; PACKARD V. PACKARD) — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Irene M. Vasquez · the will dated March 4, 2011

PURPOSE OF THIS INFORMATION SHEET
This information sheet describes what California law provides about reforming a donative instrument to correct a mistake: the rule that governed before 2015, under which extrinsic evidence could be used to show that a will was ambiguous and to clarify the ambiguity but not to correct a mistake in a will that was unambiguous; the holding of the California Supreme Court in Estate of Duke (2015) 61 Cal.4th 871 that an unambiguous will may be reformed if clear and convincing evidence establishes a mistake in the expression of the testator’s intent and the testator’s actual specific intent at the time the will was drafted; what that court said “actual specific intent” means, and the theories of mistake it expressly left for another case; the burden of proof and the reasons the court gave for setting it where it did; the Probate Code sections on the intention of the transferor and the construction of instruments that the opinion discusses, and what the opinion says about how reformation differs from construction; who decides these questions; the Restatement and Uniform Probate Code provisions the opinion reproduced; and two later published Court of Appeal decisions applying the case — one holding it does not reach a statutory specific-reference requirement for exercising a power of appointment, the other holding its reasoning extends to trusts and that a petition to reform a trust is not a trust contest. It is prepared as background in connection with the will dated March 4, 2011 of Irene M. Vasquez and any proceeding concerning that instrument in San Mateo County, California. It states what the statutes and the published opinions say. It does not say whether any instrument contains a mistake, what any evidence would prove, or what any person should do.

THE RULE BEFORE 2015 — AMBIGUITY YES, MISTAKE NO (PROB. CODE § 6111.5; ESTATE OF DUKE)
Probate Code section 6111.5, added in 1990, states when extrinsic evidence is admissible about a will: to determine whether a document constitutes a will pursuant to section 6110 or 6111, or to determine the meaning of a will or a portion of a will if the meaning is unclear. The Supreme Court in Estate of Duke described the line that statute and the case law drew. On one side, California law allowed extrinsic evidence to establish that a will is ambiguous and to clarify ambiguities in a will, citing section 6111.5 and Estate of Russell (1968) 69 Cal.2d 200, 206-213. On the other, as the parties seeking reformation acknowledged, California law did not authorize the admission of extrinsic evidence to correct a mistake in a will when the will was unambiguous, a bar the court traced to Estate of Dominici (1907) 151 Cal. 181, 186 and Estate of Page (1967) 254 Cal.App.2d 702, 719. The decision the Court of Appeal had followed in the case under review, Estate of Barnes (1965) 63 Cal.2d 580, had stated the limit in a sentence the 2015 opinion quotes back: a court may not write a will which the testator did not write. Whether the will dated March 4, 2011 of Irene M. Vasquez is ambiguous, and what evidence would bear on that, are questions this sheet does not answer.

THE 2015 HOLDING — AN UNAMBIGUOUS WILL MAY BE REFORMED (ESTATE OF DUKE)
Estate of Duke granted review to reconsider the historical rule that extrinsic evidence is inadmissible to reform an unambiguous will, concluded that the categorical bar on reformation of wills is not justified, and held that an unambiguous will may be reformed if clear and convincing evidence establishes that the will contains a mistake in the expression of the testator’s intent at the time the will was drafted and also establishes the testator’s actual specific intent at the time the will was drafted. The concluding paragraph restates the holding in the same two-element form. Before reaching the merits the court asked whether the Legislature’s work in this field foreclosed the change, and answered that the Legislature had codified judicial expansions of the admissibility of evidence about a testator’s intent without restricting the courts’ authority to develop the common law, so that the court could continue to develop the law concerning the admissibility of evidence to assist in the determination of the testator’s intent when the language of the document is clear on its face. The judgment was reversed and the case remanded for the probate court to consider the extrinsic evidence. Whether the will dated March 4, 2011 of Irene M. Vasquez could be reformed under this holding is not a question this sheet answers.

WHAT MUST BE PROVED — MISTAKE IN EXPRESSION AND ACTUAL SPECIFIC INTENT
The opinion defines the second element in a footnote appended to its statement of the issue: a testator’s actual specific intent is the particular disposition of assets the testator intended to set forth in the will. Applying that definition, the court identified two features of the charities’ theory that made it a theory of reformation. First, the alleged mistake concerned the testator’s intent at the time he wrote the will; the court observed that if his only intent then was to address the disposition of his estate in the circumstances in which he died before his wife or they died simultaneously, the will accurately reflected his intent, and any mistake would lie in his later failure to modify the will after her death — a mistake not related to the will sought to be reformed. Second, the alleged mistake and intent were sufficiently specific: the claim was precise as to both the error and the remedy. The court described such a claim, quoting the law review article it relied on throughout, as one alleging a mistake in the rendering of terms the testator authored or approved, where the remedy has exactly the dimensions of the mistake. What Irene M. Vasquez intended when the will dated March 4, 2011 was drafted is not something this sheet addresses.

WHAT THE COURT LEFT OPEN — GENERAL AND PUTATIVE INTENT
The opinion distinguishes the claim before it from a claim that the testator held a more general intent that the will as written did not accomplish. Its example is a will that sets out exactly the gift the testator meant to make, but where a mistake about the value of the assets or the needs of the beneficiary leaves the gift inadequate for the purpose the testator had in mind. Correcting that kind of error, the court explained, would require a court to decide what the testator would have done had the mistake been known — the testator’s putative intent — rather than to restore a term the testator actually settled on. The court stated that the case before it presented only the issue of whether a will may be reformed when extrinsic evidence establishes that the will fails to set forth the actual specific intent of the testator at the time the will was executed, and expressed no opinion on the availability of reformation in cases involving claims of general and putative intent. Which side of that line any claim about the will dated March 4, 2011 of Irene M. Vasquez would fall on is not a question this sheet answers.

THE CLEAR AND CONVINCING BURDEN AND THE REASONS GIVEN FOR IT
The standard of proof carries most of the weight in the opinion’s answer to the objections raised against reformation. Answering the argument that probate litigation would multiply, the court noted that claimants have long been entitled to present extrinsic evidence to establish that a will is ambiguous despite appearing unambiguous, so probate courts already weigh such evidence, and said that as to claims framed in mistake rather than ambiguity, the heightened evidentiary standard will help the probate court to filter out weak claims. Answering the argument that Probate Code section 6110, subdivision (c)(2) — which allows a will not executed with the statutory attestation formalities to be probated on clear and convincing evidence that the testator intended the writing to be a will — was not meant to relax formalities, the court said that although section 6110 does not reduce the formalities of attestation, it reflects a judgment that formalities should not defeat the testator’s intent when clear and convincing evidence satisfies the evidentiary concerns underlying them. The court also said the remedy would not make estate planning less certain, and quoted the view that no draftsman would plan to rely on a rule of litigation when proper drafting can spare its expense and hazard. What any particular evidence about the will dated March 4, 2011 would establish is not something this sheet evaluates.

REFORMATION IS NOT CONSTRUCTION (PROB. CODE §§ 21102, 21120)
Probate Code section 21102 provides that the intention of the transferor as expressed in the instrument controls the legal effect of the dispositions made in the instrument, that the rules of construction in that part apply where the intention of the transferor is not indicated by the instrument, and — in language the Legislature added in 2002 on the recommendation of the Law Revision Commission — that nothing in the section limits the use of extrinsic evidence, to the extent otherwise authorized by law, to determine the intention of the transferor. Section 21120 states two rules of construction, including that preference is to be given to an interpretation of an instrument that will prevent intestacy or failure of a transfer. Estate of Duke drew a line between construing an instrument and reforming it: the will itself is among the evidence to be considered, but when reformation rather than construction is at issue, the rules of construction — which address disposition where the testator’s intention is not reflected in the will — do not apply where extrinsic evidence supplies the missing terms. Other interpretive doctrines are likewise supplanted: although a disinheritance clause cannot prevent heirs from taking by intestacy, any intent reflected in such a clause may be relevant when reformation is sought. Which of these provisions bears on the will dated March 4, 2011 is not a question this sheet answers.

THE PURPOSES THE COURT IDENTIFIED — INTENT, UNJUST ENRICHMENT, PARITY AMONG INSTRUMENTS
Four propositions carry the opinion’s justification of the remedy. The first is its object: the purpose of reformation is to carry out the wishes of the testator, and the remedy reflects no judgment other than a preference for disposition pursuant to those wishes — the court’s answer to the argument that reformation attacks the laws of intestacy. The second concerns the will formalities: the court said stringent adherence to formalities should not be allowed to obscure the ultimate purpose of the statute of wills, which is to transfer an estate in accordance with the testator’s intent. The third is unjust enrichment: if a testator did not intend to devise property to a particular party, that party’s receipt of the property as a result of a mistake constitutes unjust enrichment. The fourth is parity among estate planning instruments: because reformation was already available for trusts and other donative documents, allowing it for those but never for wills appeared to favor those with the means to plan around probate, and denying it seemed particularly harsh as to people who write wills without the assistance of counsel and are more likely to overlook flaws in the expression of their intent. This sheet does not apply any of these propositions to the will dated March 4, 2011 of Irene M. Vasquez.

expectedJSON.body: This information sheet describes what California law provides about reforming a donative instrument to correct a mistake: the rule that governed before 2015, under which extrinsic evidence could be used to show that a will was ambiguous and to clarify the ambiguity but not to correct a mistake in a will that was unambiguous; the holding of the California Supreme Court in Estate of Duke (2015) 61 Cal.4th 871 that an unambiguous will may be reformed if clear and convincing evidence establishes a mistake in the expression of the testator’s intent and the testator’s actual specific intent at the time the will was drafted; what that court said “actual specific intent” means, and the theories of mistake it expressly left for another case; the burden of proof and the reasons the court gave for setting it where it did; the Probate Code sections on the intention of the transferor and the construction of instruments that the opinion discusses, and what the opinion says about how reformation differs from construction; who decides these questions; the Restatement and Uniform Probate Code provisions the opinion reproduced; and two later published Court of Appeal decisions applying the case — one holding it does not reach a statutory specific-reference requirement for exercising a power of appointment, the other holding its reasoning extends to trusts and that a petition to reform a trust is not a trust contest. It is prepared as background in connection with the will dated March 4, 2011 of Irene M. Vasquez and any proceeding concerning that instrument in San Mateo County, California. It states what the statutes and the published opinions say. It does not say whether any instrument contains a mistake, what any evidence would prove, or what any person should do.

Probate Code section 6111.5, added in 1990, states when extrinsic evidence is admissible about a will: to determine whether a document constitutes a will pursuant to section 6110 or 6111, or to determine the meaning of a will or a portion of a will if the meaning is unclear. The Supreme Court in Estate of Duke described the line that statute and the case law drew. On one side, California law allowed extrinsic evidence to establish that a will is ambiguous and to clarify ambiguities in a will, citing section 6111.5 and Estate of Russell (1968) 69 Cal.2d 200, 206-213. On the other, as the parties seeking reformation acknowledged, California law did not authorize the admission of extrinsic evidence to correct a mistake in a will when the will was unambiguous, a bar the court traced to Estate of Dominici (1907) 151 Cal. 181, 186 and Estate of Page (1967) 254 Cal.App.2d 702, 719. The decision the Court of Appeal had followed in the case under review, Estate of Barnes (1965) 63 Cal.2d 580, had stated the limit in a sentence the 2015 opinion quotes back: a court may not write a will which the testator did not write. Whether the will dated March 4, 2011 of Irene M. Vasquez is ambiguous, and what evidence would bear on that, are questions this sheet does not answer.

expectedJSON.body: Four propositions carry the opinion’s justification of the remedy. The first is its object: the purpose of reformation is to carry out the wishes of the testator, and the remedy reflects no judgment other than a preference for disposition pursuant to those wishes — the court’s answer to the argument that reformation attacks the laws of intestacy. The second concerns the will formalities: the court said stringent adherence to formalities should not be allowed to obscure the ultimate purpose of the statute of wills, which is to transfer an estate in accordance with the testator’s intent. The third is unjust enrichment: if a testator did not intend to devise property to a particular party, that party’s receipt of the property as a result of a mistake constitutes unjust enrichment. The fourth is parity among estate planning instruments: because reformation was already available for trusts and other donative documents, allowing it for those but never for wills appeared to favor those with the means to plan around probate, and denying it seemed particularly harsh as to people who write wills without the assistance of counsel and are more likely to overlook flaws in the expression of their intent. This sheet does not apply any of these propositions to the will dated March 4, 2011 of Irene M. Vasquez.

Section 12.1 of the Restatement provides that a donative document, though unambiguous, may be reformed to conform the text to the donor’s intention if it is established by clear and convincing evidence that a mistake of fact or law, whether in expression or inducement, affected specific terms of the document, and what the donor’s intention was. The court also recorded a Washington statute and a Connecticut decision permitting correction on a clear and convincing showing. It then added a limit: it had no occasion to consider the extent to which the reformation remedies authorized in other jurisdictions or proposed by the Restatement and the Uniform Probate Code are similar to the remedy it was authorizing. Neither the Restatement nor the uniform act is California law, and this sheet does not apply either to the will dated March 4, 2011.

expectedJSON.body: Probate Code section 632 provides that where the creating instrument expressly directs that a power of appointment be exercised by an instrument making a specific reference to the power or to the instrument that created it, the power can be exercised only by an instrument containing the required reference. Section 631 lets a court excuse some failures to follow the formal requirements a donor specified, but its subdivision (b) states that the section does not permit a court to excuse compliance with a specific reference requirement under section 632. In Estate of Eimers the Court of Appeal restated the reformation rule — a will may be reformed to conform to the testator’s intent if clear and convincing evidence establishes that the will contains a mistake in the testator’s expression of intent at the time the will was drafted — and then held the rule inapplicable. The decedent’s holographic will gave away his trust shares but did not refer to the power of appointment the trust conferred. The court said the question was not what the decedent intended but whether a court may reform a will to excuse noncompliance with sections 631(b) and 632, concluded that creating a reference from extrinsic evidence would nullify the statutory requirement, and stated that where discerning donative intent is not the issue, the reformation case does not apply, and a donor’s intent alone cannot trump the requirements of the law. Whether any statute imposes such a requirement on the will dated March 4, 2011 is not a question this sheet answers.

expectedJSON.body: The 2015 decision concerned a will. In Packard v. Packard the Court of Appeal held that although Estate of Duke involved a will, its logic applies equally to the reformation of a trust, pointing out that the Supreme Court had itself relied on decisions allowing extrinsic evidence to correct errors in trusts, including one described as allowing reformation after the trustors’ deaths to correct a drafting error. The Court of Appeal stated the resulting rule in the same two-element form: reformation of a trust is permitted even where the language appears facially unambiguous, so long as clear and convincing evidence establishes that the trust contains a mistake in the donor’s expression of intent at the time it was drafted and the donor’s actual specific intent at that time. It added that a beneficiary may petition the probate court to reform a trust that, due to a mistake, does not accurately reflect the trustor’s intent. The petition there alleged that an amendment dividing the estate “one-half” did not capture the trustor’s intent that his two sons share equally. Whether the will dated March 4, 2011 of Irene M. Vasquez contains any mistake is not a question this sheet answers.

expectedJSON.body: The question actually decided in Packard v. Packard was procedural: whether a petition to reform a trust amendment was a trust contest subject to the 120-day limitations period that runs from a trustee’s notification under Probate Code section 16061.7. The court held it was not, reasoning that a reformation petition does not question the validity of the instrument but seeks to determine and implement the trustor’s intent. It rejected the argument that a petition should be treated as a contest when the language it targets looks unambiguous, observing that whether a filing is a contest or a request to reform cannot depend on how persuasive the extrinsic evidence is, because that goes to the merits, and that a meritless reformation petition is still a reformation petition. It also said that earlier descriptions of a “contest” as any proceeding designed to thwart the testator’s expressed wishes could not, after 2015, be read to make every reformation petition a contest. The court expressed no opinion on the merits, holding only that the petitioner must be given the opportunity to prove the trustor’s intent by clear and convincing evidence. How any deadline or no-contest clause would apply to the will dated March 4, 2011 is not a question this sheet answers.
